chunks: My father narrated to us, may God be pleased with him, saying: Muhammad ibn Yahya al-Attar narrated to us, from Al-Hussein ibn Ishaq al-Tajir, from Ali ibn Mahzyar, from Al-Hussein ibn Sa'id, from Fudalah ibn Ayyub, from Isma'il ibn Abi Ziyad, from Abu Abdillah, from his father, peace be upon them both.

He said: Abu Dharr - may God have mercy on him - cried from the fear of God, the Exalted, until his eyesight failed. He was told to him: 'O Abu Dharr, if you were to supplicate to God to heal your eyesight,' he said: 'I am preoccupied with it, and it is not my greatest concern.' They asked: 'What preoccupies you from it?' He said: 'The two great [things]: Paradise and the Hellfire.'

key_terms.اشْتَكَى بَصَرَهُ: His eyesight failed/complained of his eyes

ai.seo_question: What did Abu Dharr consider more important than healing his eyesight?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Saduq highlights Abu Dharr’s asceticism by illustrating how his intense contemplation of the Hereafter (akhira) superseded concern for worldly health, a hallmark of the early Shia emphasis on *khushu'* and *muraqaba*. This narrative serves as a practical model for believers to prioritize spiritual awareness over physical comfort, reinforcing the theological weight of Paradise and Hellfire as the primary motivators for righteous action.
